newsitem.title: UK: CME looks at Austrian TV, but no decision.
newsitem.headline: CME looks at Austrian TV, but no decision.

text.p: Central European Media Enterprises Ltd, the burgeoning central and Eastern European television empire, will examine opportunities to enter the commercial television market in Austria, but it is premature to make any decision, chief executive Leonard Fertig said.

"There are reasons why it would be very appealing and reasons why it would be very unappealing," Fertig told Reuters in an interview on Thursday. "We're evaluating the situation," he added. "But we don't know which way we will go."

Austria on Wednesday unveiled a draft law that would open the market to private radio and television stations and break the monopoly of state-owned ORF. Austria is one of the last strongholds of state-controlled broadcasting.

But Fertig, in an interview at his modestly sized and furnished office at CME's headquarters in London's Soho district, said Austria's differences from CME's typical post-Communist markets would present both advantages and disadvantages.
"Austria is clearly a fairly developed country," he said. "It's not like the post-communist countries in that income levels are very high."

But while Austria has no private television networks of its own, it does receive German-language programming from neighboring countries via cable and satellite, meaning it is a market where competition would be present from day one. In addition, said Fertig, many licence rights to German programming and broadcast events are already locked up, making it a more expensive market.
CME has made no bones about its expansionist interests. But its interests remain squarely in the post-communist central and Eastern European world.

CME currently operates national television stations in the Czech Republic -- home to its flagship station TV Nova, launched in February 1994 -- Romania, Slovenia, Slovakia and Ukraine. It has a regional television operation in Poland and is due to launch a national station there next October.

It is a partner in a local television station in Germany, a troubled operation where CME and its three partners are currently seeking a new strategic partner. CME is also bidding for a national TV licence in Hungary.
Virtually the whole of central and Eastern Europe appears to be a possibility for future development.
"We're looking at the Baltics. We don't have anything that we are prepared to announce today," Fertig said. "We're looking at additional opportunities in the Balkans.

"We're looking at other opportunities in the former Soviet Union," he added. "Of course we're looking at Russia. ... We don't necessarily know when and if we will do something in a country such as Bulgaria, because of the economy. But we have people who work in these places, and when the timing is right in our view that's when we pick up and announce things."
